chunks.section: Two for the Price of One: Curvature-Aware Pruning Preserves Influence Functions Too
chunks.text: Mehdi Makni 1 Natalia Ponomareva 2 Rahul Mazumder 1 1 Operations Research Center, Massachusetts Institute of Technology 2 Google Research † † thanks: Corresponding author: mmakni@mit.edu

Post-training pruning enables efficient deployment, but conventional methods do not explicitly preserve internal-gradient alignment between sparse and dense models. We study novel connections between downstream performance of compressed models and the ability to retain gradient information via influence-function preservation. Central to this connection is a curvature-aware objective that accounts for both layer activations and backpropagated gradients. Despite its promise, this objective remains underexplored in pruning due to a lack of efficient solvers. We introduce CACTUS , a novel ADMM-based optimizer supporting both pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank decompositions of pre-trained weights. Compared to LLM-Surgeon which targets the same objective, CACTUS can achieve over an order-of-magnitude speedup. At 50 % 50\% pruning of Qwen3-4B, CACTUS reduces the C4 perplexity gap to the dense model by 45 % 45\% , improves compressed-to-dense per-sample gradient cosine similarity on WikiText-2 from 0.670 0.670 to 0.755 0.755 , and runs over 28 × 28\times faster than LLM-Surgeon on substantially weaker hardware. By preserving influence functions, CACTUS supports effective data selection. On Llama-3.2-3B, fine-tuning a fresh dense model on the 5 % 5\% of data selected by CACTUS achieves 49.44 % 49.44\% accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard, compared with 47.22 % 47.22\% using ALPS and 49.54 % 49.54\% using dense-model selection. Finally, integrating CACTUS with LoGRA, a recent gradient-projection strategy, on Qwen3-4B with MLP layers pruned to 2:4 sparsity and a rank-64 correction retains a 0.711 0.711 cosine alignment with dense LoGRA-projected C4 gradients.

Large Language Models (LLMs) ( Achiam et al., 2023 ; Dubey et al., 2024 ; Google, 2023 ) have driven advances in reasoning, code, and mathematics, but their sheer size, often measured in billions of parameters, makes both deployment and downstream inference expensive. These costs have motivated two parallel research threads that have advanced largely independently. The first thread is post-training pruning . Methods such as SparseGPT ( Frantar and Alistarh, 2023 ) , WANDA ( Sun et al., 2024 ) , and ALPS ( Meng et al., 2024 ) use a small calibration dataset to minimize the layerwise-reconstruction error ‖ 𝐗𝐖 − 𝐗 ​ 𝐖 ^ ‖ F 2 {\|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{X}\widehat{\mathbf{W}}\|_{F}^{2}} subject to a structural constraint, where 𝐗 \mathbf{X} contains input activations and 𝐖 \mathbf{W} and 𝐖 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{W}} are the dense and compressed weights, and ∥ ⋅ ∥ F \|\cdot\|_{F} is the Frobenius norm. Pruning (pure sparsity) zeroes out the weights in an unstructured pattern or in hardware-friendly n n : m m patterns that keep n n nonzeros in each contiguous block of m m weights; the common 2 2 : 4 4 case is natively accelerated by recent NVIDIA sparse Tensor Cores ( Zhou et al., 2021 ) . Sparse-plus-low-rank (SLR) compression, denoted in this paper by ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) , combines a sparse backbone 𝐒 \mathbf{S} with a low-rank correction 𝐋 \mathbf{L} under the same framework, improving compression-utility tradeoffs over either component alone ( Zhang and Papyan, 2025 ; Makni et al., 2025 ; Makni et al., 2026 ) .

The layerwise-reconstruction procedure above matches each layer’s outputs given its input activations and is therefore gradient-blind to the LLM loss (see Figure 1 ). LLM-Surgeon ( van der Ouderaa et al., 2024 ) (pruning) and YAQA ( Tseng et al., 2026 ) (quantization) additionally incorporate downstream gradients from the calibration dataset. This curvature-aware objective improves model quality, but its optimization can require multiple GPU hours per model (LLM-Surgeon in Table 2 ), limiting its adoption. Our solver minimizes the curvature-aware loss function more than an order of magnitude faster than LLM-Surgeon while improving perplexity ( Table 2 ). It also extends beyond pure pruning to curvature-aware ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) compression. Figure 3 studies Llama-3-8B with 2 2 : 4 4 sparsity and a rank-256 correction, matching the ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) configuration with serving speed and memory gains reported by Mozaffari et al. Applications include data attribution ( Pruthi et al., 2020 ; Park et al., 2023 ) , training-data selection ( Xia et al., 2024 ) , model debugging and provenance ( Grosse et al., 2023 ) , and machine unlearning. At LLM scale, evaluating this expression is prohibitively expensive. Existing methods reduce the cost on two fronts: (i) inverse-Hessian approximations (Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (KFAC) ( Martens and Grosse, 2015 ; Grosse et al., 2023 ) , its eigenvalue-corrected variant (EK-FAC), identity-Hessian as in TracIn ( Pruthi et al., 2020 ) , Adam-style preconditioners), and (ii) on the gradient side: random or architecture-aware gradient sketches (TRAK ( Park et al., 2023 ) , Low-rank Gradient Approximation (LoGRA) ( Choe et al., 2025 ) ); see Section 4 . These methods still require per-sample gradient computations , which remain costly for large models and datasets.

IProX ( Chen et al., 2026 ) introduced compressed-model proxies : with the idea of computing influence estimates using a smaller surrogate model whose gradients mimic those of the dense model. They show that minimizing the curvature-aware objective, also used by LLM-Surgeon, helps preserve per-sample gradients. IProX instantiates this idea using low-rank proxies with a two-stage pipeline: (i) each weight matrix is approximated by a product of two smaller matrices, obtained through a closed-form weighted singular value decomposition (SVD), termed influence-preserving SVD (IPSVD); and (ii) gradient-alignment distillation further adapts the low-rank proxy. In this paper, we study the connection between these two different research threads for pruning. The bridge is the curvature-aware objective in Equation 1 , and the enabler is a single algorithm that makes it practical for both high-quality pruning and influence-preserving sparse proxies. Here, influence preservation means retaining the dense model’s gradient-based influence estimates after compression. This is the sense in which the paper offers “Two for the Price of One.” Our main contributions can be summarized as follows.

The updates are derived in Section 2 . With this new unifying algorithm, we make contributions in model compression on two fronts: preserving downstream utility and influence function preservation. 2. Compression Quality. On Llama-3.2-1B at 50 % 50\% compression, CACTUS reduces the C4 perplexity gap to the dense model by 25 % 25\% for pure pruning and 28 % 28\% for ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) decompositions relative to the strongest corresponding baseline. Additionally, it maintains its advantage at different compression ratios, architectures, and model sizes (see Tables 2 , 9 , 13 , 12 and 11 ). In particular, we show in Table 14 that CACTUS reduces the C4 perplexity gap to dense by over 25 % 25\% compared to SparseGPT under 2 : 4 2{:}4 sparsity for Qwen3.8-27B.

3. Influence Preservation. On Llama-3.2-1B at 50 % 50\% pruning, CACTUS improves the cosine similarity between compressed and dense per-example gradients on WikiText-2 from 0.445 0.445 (LLM-Surgeon) to 0.512 0.512 ( Table 7 ). We then use pruned models with 50 % 50\% sparsity to select 5 % 5\% of data from an instruction-tuning mixture for fine-tuning a fresh Llama-3.2-3B model. CACTUS selected subset overlaps the dense model’s selection by 54.13 % 54.13\% , compared with 52.24 % 52.24\% for ALPS, and yields 49.44 % 49.44\% versus 47.22 % 47.22\% BBH accuracy ( Table 3 ). On Qwen3-4B, compressing MLP layers to 2 : 4 2{:}4 sparsity with a rank- 64 64 correction retains a cosine similarity of 0.711 0.711 between compressed and dense per-example gradients on C4, measured using the same LoGRA projection.

One-shot pruning and low-rank decompositions for LLMs. Post-training one-shot compression is a training-free paradigm popularized by SparseGPT ( Frantar and Alistarh, 2023 ) , which compresses a pretrained LLM layer-by-layer on a small calibration set by minimizing the layerwise reconstruction error ‖ 𝐗𝐖 − 𝐗 ​ 𝐖 ^ ‖ F 2 \|\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{X}\widehat{\mathbf{W}}\|_{F}^{2} subject to a structural constraint on 𝐖 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{W}} ; methods differ along two axes: the constraint family and the per-layer solver. Pure sparsity : SparseGPT ( Frantar and Alistarh, 2023 ) uses a sequential column-based sparsification scheme: after sparsifying one column, the remaining weights are updated to compensate for the incurred error, while ALPS ( Meng et al., 2024 ) formulates the same problem as a constrained quadratic problem solved by the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) ( Boyd et al., 2011 ) . Pure low-rank : SVD-LLM(W) ( Wang et al., 2025 ) uses a whitened Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to minimize layerwise reconstruction error; ASVD ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) instead scales input channels using activation statistics before SVD. Sparse + low-rank ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) : OATS ( Zhang and Papyan, 2025 ) and Hassle-free ( Makni et al., 2025 ) alternate a sparse fitting step with a low-rank projection step; OATS scores weights using a per-row activation-norm criterion whereas Hassle-free uses the full input correlation matrix. 3BASiL ( Makni et al., 2026 ) runs a multi-block ADMM that jointly minimizes the sparse and low-rank components simultaneously. Our method CACTUS differs from all these layerwise reconstruction algorithms by incorporating downstream gradients in its objective, making it curvature-aware rather than gradient-blind .

LLM-Surgeon ( van der Ouderaa et al., 2024 ) and IProX ( Chen et al., 2026 ) arrive at the curvature-aware objective ‖ 𝐗 ⁡ ( 𝐖 − 𝐖 ^ ) ​ 𝐀 ⊤ ‖ F 2 \|\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{W}-\widehat{\mathbf{W}})\mathbf{A}^{\top}\|_{F}^{2} from different motivations: LLM-Surgeon approximates the change in model loss, whereas IProX seeks to preserve gradient information for influence estimation ( Appendices A and 5 ). LLM-Surgeon targets pure pruning through curvature-based weight selection and correlated corrections over multiple rounds; IProX constructs a pure low-rank proxy through a weighted SVD followed by gradient-alignment fine-tuning. YAQA ( Tseng et al., 2026 ) is a related approach which applies downstream curvature to weight-only quantization. Its curvature-based error feedback is conceptually closer to LLM-Surgeon’s error compensation than to our ADMM splitting procedure. CACTUS differs from these prior methods as it optimizes the curvature-aware loss for pruning and ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) using multi-block ADMM with efficient subroutines: a closed-form Sylvester solve in cached eigenbases, sparsity projections, and a randomized-SVD-based low-rank approximation ( Section 2.2 ). On Qwen3-4B at 50 % 50\% compression, CACTUS -prune is over 28 × 28\times faster than five-shot LLM-Surgeon † , using one L40 rather than two A100 GPUs ( Tables 9 and C ). Our pruning and ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) representations also achieve substantially lower perplexity than IProX’s aligned low-rank proxy ( Table 7 ).

In this paper, we first highlight the connection between downstream utility and influence preservation through the curvature-aware objective introduced in Equation 1 . Our new algorithm CACTUS makes optimizing this objective practical for modern LLM pruning as well as ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) decomposition tasks. It runs at a substantially lower cost compared to prior state-of-the-art curvature-aware pruning methods. Across various compression settings, model architectures, and gradient projection strategies, CACTUS consistently improves downstream utility while retaining gradient fidelity. Limitations. In this paper, we focus on pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) compression. Extending our ADMM framework to quantization and mixed quantization-sparsity settings are directions for future work, especially when reparameterizations (e.g., rotations) change gradient geometry. We also only consider uniform compression budgets; it would be interesting to design specialized methods that can allocate sparsity and rank non-uniformly across the entire LLM layers. Additionally, we do not study post-compression refinements like full-model or LoRA-style finetuning. These may trade off deployment quality and gradient alignment fidelity in different ways. We leave these interesting follow-up research directions for future work.

All one-shot baselines are run in the same layerwise compression framework and with the same calibration samples, except when a method explicitly includes a post-compression stage. SparseGPT , ALPS , SVD-LLM(W) (simple activation-aware low-rank fitting without sequential factor refinement or post-compression fine-tuning), OATS , and 3BASiL use activation-only objectives using 𝐇 \mathbf{H} , whereas IPSVD , IProX , LLM-Surgeon , and CACTUS use 𝐆 \mathbf{G} as well. For ( 𝐒 + 𝐋 ) (\mathbf{S}+\mathbf{L}) baselines at target compression ratio c c , we match total parameter budget using the same layerwise rank allocation r ℓ = ⌊ η ⁡ ( 1 − c ) ​ m ℓ ​ n ℓ / ( m ℓ + n ℓ ) ⌋ r_{\ell}=\lfloor\eta(1-c)m_{\ell}n_{\ell}/(m_{\ell}+n_{\ell})\rfloor with η = 0.3 \eta=0.3 ; for named structured settings such as ( 2 : 4 + r ​ 256 ) (2{:}4{+}r256) , the sparsity pattern and rank are fixed exactly as specified. For LLM-Surgeon, we use row-wise correlated weight updates ( max_correlate=-1 ), jointly accounting for the pruned weights within each row when computing weight compensation, for both unstructured and 2:4 pruning. We also employ the five-shot setting described in Section 3.1 , since the one-shot unstructured pruning on Llama3.2-1B produced weak results. For Qwen3-4B model under 2:4 sparsity on MLP layers, one-shot results are competitive, so we report both one-shot and five-shot results.

We estimate activation and gradient covariance factors from 128 128 C4 calibration sequences at sequence length 2048 2048 (see effect of number of calibration data points at Table 15 ). This is a standard calibration set introduced by SparseGPT [ Frantar and Alistarh, 2023 ] and adopted by most layerwise reconstruction algorithms like ALPS [ Meng et al., 2024 ] . We evaluate language model utility with C4 and WikiText-2 perplexity at sequence length 2048 2048 . Influence-preservation metrics use projected per-example gradients (via TRAK’s fast_jl ) with the same seeded projection. Thus, TracIn entries are computed as ⟨ Π ​ g i , Π ​ g j ⟩ \langle\Pi g_{i},\Pi g_{j}\rangle under a fixed JL sketch Π \Pi , which preserves inner products and ensures dense and compressed gradients are compared in the same projected space. The per-sample gradients are sampled from n tr = 1000 n_{\text{tr}}=1000 C4 training sequences (different from calibration samples) and n te = 100 n_{\text{te}}=100 WikiText-2 test sequences, both at sequence length 512 512 .

We follow the LESS [ Xia et al., 2024 ] data-selection procedure on its released FLAN-v2, CoT, Dolly, and OpenAssistant mixture (270,679 candidates), comparing dense and compressed scoring models. Scorers share a 5 % 5\% warm-up sample and train LoRA adapters on attention q / k / v / o q/k/v/o projections for four epochs. Warm-up and target training use learning rate 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} , effective batch size 128 128 , sequence length 2048 2048 , cosine decay, and 3 % 3\% learning-rate warm-up. Similar to the LESS framework, we apply a shared 8192 8192 -dimensional TRAK projection to Adam-aware candidate updates and ordinary query gradients in the LoRA parameter space.
